chunks: How to spec an MCU. The question: How do you spec an MCU? What specs do you look for?
Specifying an MCU means turning what your product must do into numbers, and then choosing the smallest chip that meets them with room to spare.
Start from the requirements, not a datasheet (the maker's spec sheet). Work out how much processing, memory, input/output and battery life you need.
Then check candidate chips against those totals. Too small a chip hits a wall late in the project. Too big a chip wastes cost and power.
Picture choosing a moving truck. You first measure what you must move: the volume of boxes, the heaviest item, and how far you are going.
Then you add some extra room, because you will always find more stuff. A truck that is too small means a second trip halfway through.
A truck that is far too big costs more to rent and burns more fuel.
For frequent tasks (left) the part with lower energy per task (B: 6 µC against 10 µC) wins; for rare tasks (right) sleep current dominates and part A wins.
The crossover is where 4 micro C over T equals 14 micro A . The lesson is to model your own duty cycle before choosing on a single datasheet figure.
Cycle budget: how many clock ticks the processor has for each pass of its main task. Headroom: spare capacity left over for new features and surprises.
Peripheral: a built-in hardware block such as a timer, converter or serial port ("How an MCU talks to peripherals").
Pin multiplexing: one physical pin can serve several functions, but only one at a time. Sleep current: the tiny current the chip draws while idle, which drives battery life.
Errata: the maker's list of known bugs in the chip.
A motor control loop runs 20,000 times per second on a 72 megahertz chip. The cycle budget is 72 000 000 over 20 000 equals 3 600 ticks per pass.
If the algorithm needs 1,800 ticks, it uses half, which leaves good headroom. For memory, say the program (firmware) is 64 KB (kilobytes).
Safe updates need room for a second copy, plus a 16 KB starter program (a bootloader) that picks which copy runs.
That is 2 times 64 plus 16 equals 144 KB, so you pick the next size up, 256 KB. That is the whole idea.
"I derive the spec from the requirements. CPU: cycles per loop, such as 3,600 cycles per 20 kilohertz iteration at 72 megahertz, with at most about half used.
Memory: flash for code, bootloader and update image, RAM for buffers, plus 30–50% margin.
Peripherals: enough timers, ADC channels and rate, buses and DMA, checked against pin muxing. Power: supply range, µA/MHz and sleep current.
Then temperature grade, package, ecosystem, errata, cost and availability, ideally within a pin-compatible family."
